framework.name: InSPECT

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?
themes.example: Andean terraces made steep slopes more usable for farming.

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?
themes.example: Examination preparation favored families that could afford education.

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

questions.prompt: Why did many medieval European monarchs depend on local nobles?
choices: Nobles controlled land, so kings had no recognized legal claim to rule over their own kingdoms
Nobles were appointed through examinations that kings were required to accept
Nobles controlled land, armed men, and local justice that kings could not run directly
Nobles paid all royal taxes, so kings never needed revenue of their own
questions.explanation: Limited revenue and slow communication made kings rely on lords who held land and followers.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Nobles held land, but kings still claimed authority; the issue was practical control.
European nobility was largely hereditary, not selected by examination.
Limited revenue and slow communication made kings rely on lords who held land and followers.
Kings collected their own revenues, though limited ones; that limit is part of the explanation.
questions.distinguisher: The problem was practical capacity, not legal title.

questions.prompt: Which distinction between feudal relationships and manorialism is most useful?
choices: Feudalism linked elites through land and service; manorialism organized peasant labor
Feudalism applied only in towns, while manorialism applied only in monasteries
Feudalism ended in 1200, and manorialism replaced it across all of Europe
Feudalism organized peasant labor; manorialism linked elites through military service
questions.explanation: Feudal ties connected lords and vassals; manors organized production and peasant obligations.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Feudal ties connected lords and vassals; manors organized production and peasant obligations.
Both were rural arrangements centered on land.
Both continued, varying by place, through this period.
This reverses the two systems.

questions.prompt: Which example shows the Church functioning as more than a place of worship?
choices: A priest leads a procession through town on an important holy day
A monastery holds daily prayers and services for monks and local villagers
A cathedral is built in a city to hold the relics of a local saint
A monastery manages farmland, runs a school, and advises regional lords
questions.explanation: Landholding, education, and political influence show economic and social roles beyond worship.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Processions are religious observances.
Prayer services are the Church's religious role, which the question asks you to look beyond.
Relics and cathedrals are religious functions.
Landholding, education, and political influence show economic and social roles beyond worship.
questions.distinguisher: Look for economic, educational, or political roles.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes religious life in medieval Europe?
choices: Christianity dominated, and Jewish and Muslim communities enjoyed fully equal legal rights everywhere
Christianity dominated, while Jewish and Muslim communities faced both exchange and persecution
Most Europeans had converted to Islam after the Crusades brought it to the region
Religion had little effect on daily life outside monasteries and cathedrals
questions.explanation: Christian institutions were central, and minority communities contributed to trade and learning while facing restrictions and violence.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Christianity's dominance is right, but minorities faced legal restrictions and expulsions.
Christian institutions were central, and minority communities contributed to trade and learning while facing restrictions and violence.
Christianity remained the majority religion; Muslim rule existed in parts of Iberia.
Christian beliefs shaped work, holidays, law, and family life.
questions.distinguisher: Influence and diversity, with both cooperation and conflict.

questions.prompt: How could agricultural improvements contribute to town growth?
choices: Crop rotation let lords sell their manors to town merchants
Larger harvests could feed people who worked in crafts and trade
Heavy plows were made in towns, which became rich from selling them
Larger harvests could end serfdom, freeing all peasants to move to towns
questions.explanation: Surplus food supported people who did not farm, allowing towns to grow.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Rotation improved yields; it did not transfer estates to merchants.
Surplus food supported people who did not farm, allowing towns to grow.
Towns produced tools, but surplus food explains their growth better.
More food helped towns, but serfdom did not end because of harvests alone.

questions.prompt: Which explanation best connects the conditions in the passage to changing labor relations in western Europe?
choices: Plague losses made labor less valuable because fewer goods were needed
Fewer workers raised labor's bargaining power, so serfdom ended everywhere in Europe at once
Abandoned farms let lords hire more workers at lower wages than before
Fewer workers raised labor's bargaining power, while elites tried to hold wages down
questions.explanation: Boccaccio's “high and extravagant wage” reflects scarcity; laws such as England's Statute of Labourers tried to cap wages.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Demand fell in some areas, but labor became scarcer and more valuable.
Bargaining power rose, but serfdom declined unevenly over many years.
Scarce labor pushed wages up, not down.
Boccaccio's “high and extravagant wage” reflects scarcity; laws such as England's Statute of Labourers tried to cap wages.
questions.distinguisher: Scarcity strengthens bargaining, but elites push back.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Giovanni Boccaccio, Florentine writer, introduction to The Decameron, completed c. 1353, describing Florence and its countryside during the plague of 1348
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Decameron of Giovanni Boccaccio, trans. John Payne (London: Villon Society, 1886), First Day, introduction. Project Gutenberg eBook #23700.
stimulusBlocks.note: Husbandmen are farmers. Payne's 1886 English imitates older usage.
stimulusBlocks.text:
By reason whereof there remained unto those (and the number of them, both males and females, was incalculable) who fell sick, none other succour than that which they owed either to the charity of friends (and of these there were few) or the greed of servants, who tended them, allured by high and extravagant wage . . . .

throughout the scattered villages and in the fields, the poor and miserable husbandmen and their families, without succour of physician or aid of servitor, died, not like men, but well nigh like beasts, by the ways or in their tillages or about the houses, indifferently by day and night. . . . the oxen, the asses, the sheep, the goats, the swine, the fowls, nay, the very dogs, so faithful to mankind, being driven forth of their own houses, went straying at their pleasure about the fields, where the very corn was abandoned, without being cut, much less gathered in

questions.prompt: Why is the Fourth Crusade’s attack on Constantinople important for interpreting religious conflict?
choices: Political and commercial interests could lead crusaders to attack fellow Christians
Political and commercial interests caused nearly every crusade to target Christian cities instead
It showed that the Crusades ended Christian control of Jerusalem permanently
It united the Catholic and Orthodox churches under Byzantine leadership
questions.explanation: The 1204 sack of Constantinople shows motives beyond a simple Christian-versus-Muslim struggle.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: The 1204 sack of Constantinople shows motives beyond a simple Christian-versus-Muslim struggle.
Interests mattered, but most crusades targeted Muslim-ruled lands; 1204 is an important exception.
Jerusalem had already been lost to Saladin in 1187; the Fourth Crusade never reached it.
The attack deepened the split between the churches.
questions.distinguisher: An exception complicates a simple pattern.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes early Renaissance humanism?
choices: Humanism began in the monasteries of Ethiopia and spread to Italy
Humanism ended the influence of universities across Europe
Renewed classical study coexisted with Christian belief and institutions
Renewed classical study led most humanists to reject Christian belief
questions.explanation: Many humanists were devout Christians who studied classical texts alongside religious ones.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Humanism developed in Italian cities.
Universities continued and adapted to new learning.
Many humanists were devout Christians who studied classical texts alongside religious ones.
Classical study grew, but most humanists remained Christian.

questions.prompt: What commonly distinguished a serf from a free peasant?
choices: Exemption from rents, labor, and other dues
Ownership of the land that the family had farmed for generations
Military service owed as a knight to a king or great lord
Inherited duties and limits on movement tied to an estate
questions.explanation: Serfs owed hereditary obligations and often could not leave without permission.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Serfs owed rents and labor; exemption describes privilege.
Serfs worked land they did not own.
Knightly service belonged to elites, not serfs.
Serfs owed hereditary obligations and often could not leave without permission.
questions.distinguisher: Serfdom meant inherited obligations and restrictions.

choices: A tax paid by peasants to the Church
A charter granting a town self-government
Land or rights granted in return for service
A guild's rules for training apprentices
questions.explanation: A lord granted a fief to a vassal, who owed loyalty and service in return.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Payments to the Church were tithes.
Town charters were separate grants of rights.
A lord granted a fief to a vassal, who owed loyalty and service in return.
Guild rules governed crafts, not land grants.
questions.distinguisher: A fief supported a vassal's service.

questions.prompt: What does vernacular mean in literary history?
choices: A style of church architecture
A language people commonly spoke in a region
A collection of classical Greek texts translated into Latin
Latin, the language of the Church and the universities
questions.explanation: Writers such as Dante and Chaucer wrote in the everyday languages of their regions.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Vernacular refers to language, not architecture.
Writers such as Dante and Chaucer wrote in the everyday languages of their regions.
Vernacular is the opposite of classical learned languages.
Latin was the learned language; vernacular means the local spoken one.
